headline: Critical UEFI firmware flaw affects most servers globally, rated 9.5/10
summary: A severe memory-corruption vulnerability in EDK2 allows code execution before OS defenses, potentially breaking disk encryption and installing persistent malware.
details: A critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-97631, has been discovered in the TianoCore EDK II, an open-source codebase used by most server vendors and data centers for UEFI firmware. Rated 9.5/10, it allows attackers to execute code early in the boot process, before operating system defenses like Secure Boot can be activated.

The flaw resides in an ICMP component and is a memory-corruption issue that can be exploited to hijack program flow. This could grant attackers access to sensitive components like the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), potentially enabling them to break disk encryption or install other persistent malware.

The vulnerability was discovered by Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google. While a fix has been published by AMI, the availability of patch code makes it easier for advanced hackers to develop exploits. Patching UEFI firmware across millions of devices is a complex and time-consuming process.

The vulnerability stems from a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver, which handles network booting. The driver does not enforce a memory copy limit, allowing oversized ICMP error messages to overwrite adjacent data and corrupt the UEFI module.
